title: why there's fire in every church
hookLine: why there's fire in every church
last: ONE DAY THAT ISN'T YOURS TO FILL.

cards: Every building has lights now. Switches, LEDs, the glow of exit signs. And yet step into a Catholic church at noon, in a city with perfect electricity, and there's still fire.
Two candles on the altar. A tall one near the front. Rows of little flames in a side corner, flickering, somebody's coins in the box beside them.
And one small red lamp that never seems to go out. It isn't for seeing. Nobody needs a candle to read anymore.
So why is there fire in every church?

teach.h: I AM THE LIGHT OF THE WORLD.
teach.b: Start with what Jesus says in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "I am the light of the world: he that followeth me, walketh not in darkness." So a candle in a church is a small sermon without words.
Light in the dark. And every candle there has its own job. The candles on or near the altar are lit for Mass.
The tall one is the Easter candle, the paschal candle.
On the night before Easter, Catholics gather outside in the dark, light a new fire, and carry this one candle into a black church while someone sings, three times, light of Christ.
Then the flame is passed from candle to candle through the whole crowd until the room is full of light. The same candle stands near the font at baptisms, and beside the coffin at funerals.

teach.h: THE RED LAMP: HE IS HERE.
teach.b: The little red lamp is the one from day two: the sanctuary lamp, burning near the tabernacle as a sign that Christ is present there. And the rows in the corner?

Votive candles, from the Latin votum, a vow or a prayer. Someone lights one for a sick mother, a job interview, a child who's struggling, a friend who died. The flame keeps burning after they walk out the door.
Some people put it this way: the candle keeps praying after I leave. In Catholic teaching, the wax does nothing by itself.
It's a way of saying: this person matters, and I'm not done hoping.

how: Catholics light votive candles in churches for people they are praying for, keep a sanctuary lamp burning near the tabernacle, and light the paschal candle at the Easter Vigil, baptisms and funerals.

games.q: which flame is which — tap the pairs.
p: lit from new fire before Easter
lit for someone you pray for

s: church candles are left over from before electricity, and nothing more
each has a job: a sign of Christ's light, of his presence, or of someone's prayer.
the same Easter candle stands at baptisms and funerals
it marks the beginning and the end of a Christian life.
Catholics believe the wax itself does the praying
the candle is a sign of a prayer and of hope, not a charm.

games.q: it's the night before Easter. the church is completely dark and everyone's standing outside. what happens next?
o: someone flips on all the lights.
a new fire is lit, and one candle is carried in and shared.
games.why: a new fire, one tall candle, "light of Christ" sung three times, and the flame passed hand to hand until the room is full.

practice: Here's the practice. If there's a candle nearby, you can light it. If not, just picture one.
Think of one person who could use some light right now. See their face above the flame. You don't have to fix anything.
Just hold them there while it burns, breathing slowly. If you pray, you can pray for them.

wordCard.voice: Candles. Light in the dark: the Easter candle, the sanctuary lamp, and the votive flame that keeps praying after you leave. Fifteenth word.

orig.note: Latin: the light of Christ. sung three times as the Easter candle enters the dark church.

carryVoice: Your line: light a candle for someone. The flame keeps hoping after you've gone. Day fifteen.
